1-1.text: Part one. How likely? ... Probability tells us how likely something is to happen. We can use words: impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely and certain.

1-2.text: Rolling a 7 on a dice numbered 1 to 6 is impossible. Getting heads when you flip a fair coin is an even chance. The Sun rising tomorrow is certain.

1-3.text: We can also use numbers. Impossible is 0. Certain is 1. An even chance is one half, or 0.5. Every probability is somewhere from 0 to 1.

2-1.text: Part two. Working out probabilities. ... When all the outcomes are equally likely, the probability is the number of ways it can happen, divided by the total number of outcomes.

2-2.text: A fair dice has 6 equally likely outcomes. There is only one 6, so the probability of rolling a 6 is one sixth.

2-3.text: Rolling a number greater than 4 can happen 2 ways: a 5 or a 6. So the probability is two sixths, which simplifies to one third.

2-4.text: A bag has 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green counters. That is 10 counters. 5 are blue, so the probability of picking blue is five tenths, which equals one half.

3-1.text: Part three. Not happening. ... Something either happens or it doesn't. The two probabilities always add up to 1.

3-2.text: The probability of rain tomorrow is 0.3. So the probability of no rain is 1 minus 0.3, which is 0.7.

3-3.text: Back to the bag of 10 counters. The probability of green is two tenths. So the probability of not green is 1 minus two tenths, which is eight tenths, or four fifths.

4-1.text: Part four. Expected results. ... If you repeat something many times, you can work out how many times you expect an outcome: probability times number of tries.

4-2.text: Flip a fair coin 200 times. The probability of heads is one half, and one half times 200 equals 100. So we expect about 100 heads.

4-3.text: This spinner has 4 equal parts and 1 is red. Spin it 80 times: one quarter times 80 equals 20. We expect red about 20 times.

4-4.text: Real results are usually close, but not exact. And a coin has no memory: after 5 heads in a row, the chance of heads next time is still one half.

5-1.text: Part five. Two events. ... Flip two coins. List every outcome carefully: HH, HT, TH and TT. That is 4 equally likely outcomes.

5-2.text: Only one of the 4 outcomes is two heads, so the probability of two heads is one quarter.

5-3.text: Now flip a coin and roll a dice. A table helps you list every outcome without missing any.

5-4.text: The coin has 2 outcomes and the dice has 6, so there are 2 times 6, which is 12 outcomes. The probability of heads and a 6 is one twelfth.
